Extended examples

Kyungsub Lee

2026-10-20

Source: vignettes/articles/extended_example.Rmd
extended_example.Rmd

These examples extend the basic univariate and bivariate workflow in Get started. Choose a topic below. Each article loads emhawkes and defines its own model specifications and simulated data; the articles can be run independently.

Topic Examples Main features
Multi-kernel models Multi-kernel and synchronized intensity Multiple decay scales, type_col_map, shared parameters
Marked models Linear impact impact, eta, rmark, dmark
State-dependent baseline Fosset spread and Hawkes/M/infinity queue State from event counts, function-valued mu
State-dependent impact Hawkes flocking and bid-ask prices State-dependent excitation, lambda_component_n

The baseline examples are a useful starting point for state-dependent models. The impact examples then introduce event-dependent shocks and adjustments to accumulated intensity components.

Multi-kernel models

Multi-kernel model

Define and fit a model with multiple exponential kernels. Use type_col_map to associate kernel columns with event types.

Synchronized intensity model

Share parameters across component functions. This two-kernel model uses named parameters shared by mu and beta.

Marked models

Linear impact model

Add mark-dependent excitation and estimate the mark distribution. The examples cover a general impact function and the linear eta interface.

State-dependent baseline

Fosset’s state-dependent spread model

Simulate and fit spread widening and narrowing. The narrowing baseline becomes zero at the minimum spread.

A Hawkes/M/infinity queue: website visits and departures

Model visitor arrivals and departures. Hawkes arrivals increase the population, and each visitor has an exponential departure time.

State-dependent impact

Hawkes flocking model

Make excitation depend on relative counting-process levels. The impact function reads the observed event counts.

Bid-ask price model

Combine state-dependent baseline and component adjustments. The model uses marked price changes and the current lambda_component_n matrix.

Point processes with flexible residuals

FRPP-specific functionality is planned to move to the separate frpp package. Use its FRPP examples for fspec(), fsim() and ffit(). The full examples previously shown here, including the original emhawkes fitting code, are preserved in the compatibility vignette.

Simple custom-residual models can still use set_residual(), hsim() and logLik() in emhawkes. These functions remain available during the transition; this documentation change does not remove or deprecate them. For example:

library(emhawkes)
h_residual <- set_residual(
  new("hspec", mu = 0.5, alpha = 1, beta = 1.2),
  param = c(a = 0.7, ell = 1.6),
  dresidual = dtzexp, presidual = ptzexp,
  qresidual = qtzexp, rresidual = rtzexp
)
set.seed(1107)
path_residual <- hsim(h_residual, size = 100, lambda_component0 = 0)
logLik(h_residual, inter_arrival = path_residual$inter_arrival,
       lambda_component0 = 0)
#> loglikelihood 
#>      63.13951

Hawkes goodness-of-fit residual diagnostics remain part of emhawkes; see Fitting and inference.
